chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Sulayman ibn Jafar al-Jafari, from one who mentioned it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) used to say: Indeed, among the rights of the scholar is that you do not multiply questioning him, nor seize him by his garment; and when you enter upon him while a group is in his presence, greet them all, but single him out with a special greeting apart from them, and sit before him and do not sit behind him.

Do not wink with your eye, nor gesture with your hand, nor multiply saying 'so-and-so said this and so-and-so said that' in contradiction to his words, nor bore yourself from his prolonged company, for the example of the scholar is like the palm tree: you wait for it until something from it falls upon you.
And the scholar has a greater reward than the fasting one, the one standing in prayer, and the fighter in the way of God.

key_terms.التحية: The special greeting or salutation reserved for the scholar
key_terms.الصائم القائم الغازي: The fasting one, the prayer-standing one, and the fighter — highest categories of worship
key_terms.حق العالم: The rights owed to the scholar; their due respect and treatment
key_terms.في سبيل الله: In the way of God; fighting or striving for the sake of God
key_terms.مثل النخلة: Simile of the palm tree — patience in waiting for knowledge to come from the scholar

ai.seo_question: What are the rights of a scholar according to Imam Ali in al-Kafi?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (AS) enumerates the proper etiquette for a student in the presence of a scholar, covering respectful conduct (not overburdening with questions, not grabbing his clothing), proper seating, avoidance of distracting gestures, and refraining from citing contrary opinions. The hadith concludes with the analogy of the scholar as a palm tree — one must wait patiently for the fruit of knowledge — and affirms that the scholar's reward surpasses even that of the fasting worshipper and the fighter for God's cause. This teaching reflects the elevated status accorded to religious scholars in early Shia Islam, and the importance placed on maintaining the dignity of the scholar-student relationship.
